meta.titre: Linear Transformations: matrices acting on points and lines

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Pure Mathematics with Mechanics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Every time a photograph on a phone screen is rotated, mirrored or stretched, the same rule is applied to the coordinates of every point of the picture. A designer in Douala who resizes a logo for a signboard relies on exactly that. In mathematics such rules are written as matrices, and a single matrix acting on the coordinates tells you where every point, line and shape goes. At A Level the questions ask for the image of a point, of a line, or of a shape under a given matrix, for the matrix of a combination of two transformations, and for the way the area changes.

items: Two matrices are multiplied by taking each row of the left matrix with each column of the right matrix, and the product of a matrix and a column vector gives a column vector.
The determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ is $ad-bc$, and when it is not zero the inverse is $\dfrac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$.
A straight line has an equation $y=mx+c$ and the gradient through two points $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ is $\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$.
A point $(x,y)$ is written as the column vector $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}$, and a point $(x,y,z)$ in three dimensions as a column of three entries.

sections.titre: Matrices acting on points, lines and shapes
sections.contenu_markdown:
### The image of a point

A **linear transformation** $T$ obeys $T(\mathbf p+\mathbf q)=T(\mathbf p)+T(\mathbf q)$ and $T(k\mathbf p)=kT(\mathbf p)$, and it is represented by a matrix $\mathbf M$: the image of the point with column vector $\mathbf p$ is $\mathbf M\mathbf p$. In two dimensions,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}X\\Y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}ax+by\\cx+dy\end{pmatrix}
\tag{1}
$$

The **columns** of $\mathbf M$ are the images of $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. The origin always maps to itself. In three dimensions a $3\times3$ matrix acts on a column of three entries in the same way.

Standard $2\times2$ matrices:

| Transformation | Matrix |
|---|---|
| Rotation about $O$ through $\theta$ anticlockwise | $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$ |
| Reflection in the $x$-axis | $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ |
| Reflection in the line $y=x$ | $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ |
| Enlargement, scale factor $k$, centre $O$ | $\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&k\end{pmatrix}$ |

### Combining transformations

If $\mathbf A$ is applied first and $\mathbf B$ second, the single matrix is

$$
\mathbf M=\mathbf B\mathbf A
\tag{2}
$$

The matrix applied first stands **on the right**, next to the column vector. In general $\mathbf B\mathbf A\ne\mathbf A\mathbf B$.

### Determinant, area and inverse

$$
\det\mathbf M=ad-bc
\tag{3}
$$

The area of the image of any shape is $|\det\mathbf M|$ times the area of the shape. A negative determinant means that the orientation is reversed (as in a reflection). If $\det\mathbf M=0$ the plane collapses onto a line or a point and $\mathbf M$ has no inverse.

### The image of a line

If $(X,Y)$ is the image of $(x,y)$ then $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf M^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}X\\Y\end{pmatrix}$. Substitute these expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the equation of the line: the result is an equation in $X$ and $Y$, which is the image line. Do **not** just replace $x,y$ by $X,Y$.

variantes.nom: Image of a line using two points
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the matrix is easy to apply to points and you want to avoid finding an inverse.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Since a non-singular matrix sends a line to a line, take two points on the original line, find their images, and write the equation of the line through the images. For $y=2x+1$ under $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$: $(0,1)\mapsto(1,1)$ and $(1,3)\mapsto(6,5)$. The gradient is $\dfrac{5-1}{6-1}=\dfrac45$, so the image line is $Y-1=\tfrac45(X-1)$, that is $5Y=4X+1$, the same as obtained with the inverse. For a line **through the origin** $y=mx$, the single point $(1,m)$ is enough: if its image is $(X_0,Y_0)$, the image line is the line through the origin and $(X_0,Y_0)$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the point and the matrix have three coordinates.

variantes.nom: Composition and the determinant of a product
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question applies two transformations one after the other, or asks what single transformation is equivalent.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Let $\mathbf A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (rotation through $90^{\circ}$ anticlockwise about $O$) and $\mathbf B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ (reflection in the $x$-axis). Rotation first and then reflection is $\mathbf B\mathbf A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$, which sends $(1,0)$ to $(0,-1)$: it is a reflection in the line $y=-x$. Reflection first and then rotation is $\mathbf A\mathbf B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, a reflection in $y=x$. The two orders give different transformations. Determinants multiply: $\det(\mathbf B\mathbf A)=\det\mathbf B\cdot\det\mathbf A=(-1)(1)=-1$, so area is preserved and orientation is reversed.

sections.enonce_markdown: The matrix $\mathbf M=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ represents a linear transformation of the plane. Find the equation of the image of the line $y=2x+1$.

etapes.action: Write the image of a general point.
etapes.justification: Equation (1) gives the coordinates $(X,Y)$ of the image of $(x,y)$.
The line must be rewritten in terms of $X$ and $Y$, which needs $\mathbf M^{-1}$. First compute the determinant.

etapes.action: Express $x$ and $y$ in terms of $X$ and $Y$.
Substitute into the equation of the line.
etapes.justification: Every point of the image line comes from a point $(x,y)$ satisfying $y=2x+1$.

etapes.action: Check with two points and state the result.
etapes.justification: The points $(0,1)$ and $(1,3)$ lie on the original line, so their images must satisfy the new equation.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The image of the line $y=2x+1$ is the line $5Y=4X+1$, that is $Y=\dfrac{4X+1}{5}$, with gradient $\dfrac45$ and $Y$-intercept $\dfrac15$. It does not pass through the origin, because the original line does not.

items.erreur_markdown: Reading the image of $(1,0)$ under $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ as $(3,1)$, the first row.
items.pourquoi_faux: The image of $(1,0)$ is the first **column** of the matrix, because only the first entry of the vector is non-zero.

items.erreur_markdown: Finding the matrix for 'rotation $\mathbf A$, then reflection $\mathbf B$' as $\mathbf A\mathbf B$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The matrix applied first is nearest to the column vector, so it must be on the right of the product.
items.correction_markdown: The combined matrix is $\mathbf B\mathbf A$. With $\mathbf A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ the product $\mathbf B\mathbf A$ is a reflection in $y=-x$, but $\mathbf A\mathbf B$ is a reflection in $y=x$.

items.erreur_markdown: Stating that the image of $y=2x+1$ is $Y=2X+1$ (replacing $x,y$ by $X,Y$).
items.pourquoi_faux: The transformation moves points, so $(X,Y)$ is not the same as $(x,y)$, and the equation of the line changes.
items.correction_markdown: Use $x=X-Y$, $y=-2X+3Y$ from the inverse, giving $5Y=4X+1$, or take two points on the line and map them.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that a matrix with $\det\mathbf M=-1$ changes areas by a factor of $-1$.
items.pourquoi_faux: An area cannot be negative; the sign of the determinant records orientation, not size.
items.correction_markdown: The area scale factor is $|\det\mathbf M|=1$, and the negative sign shows that the orientation is reversed, as in a reflection.

items.erreur_markdown: Claiming that every line is mapped onto a line through the origin because the origin is an invariant point.
items.pourquoi_faux: The origin is invariant, but an invertible matrix sends only the origin to the origin, so a line that misses the origin has an image that also misses it.
items.correction_markdown: For an invertible matrix, a line through the origin maps to a line through the origin, and a line not through the origin maps to a line not through the origin, as with $5Y=4X+1$.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Find the image of the point $(1,-2,3)$ under the transformation with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\1&3&2\\0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$. (b) Find the image of $(4,2)$ under $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and describe the transformation.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Row by column: $2\cdot1+(-1)(-2)+0\cdot3=4$; $1\cdot1+3(-2)+2\cdot3=1$; $0\cdot1+1\cdot(-2)+4\cdot3=10$. The image is **$(4,1,10)$**.

(b) $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0-2\\4+0\end{pmatrix}$, so the image is **$(-2,4)$**. The matrix is the rotation matrix with $\theta=90^{\circ}$ (cosine $0$, sine $1$): an anticlockwise rotation through $90^{\circ}$ about $O$.

items.enonce_markdown: A transformation has matrix $\mathbf N=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&5\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the equation of the image of the line $y=x-2$. (b) Find $\det\mathbf N$ and state what it tells you about areas and orientation.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\det\mathbf N=1\cdot5-2\cdot3=-1$, so $\mathbf N^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{-1}\begin{pmatrix}5&-2\\-3&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-5&2\\3&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Hence $x=-5X+2Y$ and $y=3X-Y$.

Substituting into $y=x-2$: $3X-Y=-5X+2Y-2$, so $8X+2=3Y$. The image line is **$3Y=8X+2$**. (Check: $(0,-2)\mapsto(-4,-10)$ and $3(-10)=-30=8(-4)+2$.)

(b) $\det\mathbf N=$ **$-1$**. Areas are unchanged because $|\det\mathbf N|=1$, and the orientation is reversed because the determinant is negative.

items.enonce_markdown: A linear transformation $T$ maps the point $(1,1)$ to $(5,3)$ and the point $(1,-1)$ to $(1,-1)$. (a) Find the matrix $\mathbf T$ of the transformation. (b) Show that each of the lines $y=-x$ and $y=\tfrac12x$ is mapped onto itself. (c) Find the area of the image of the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(2,0)$ and $(0,3)$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Let $\mathbf T=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$. Then $a+b=5$, $a-b=1$, $c+d=3$, $c-d=-1$. Adding and subtracting: $a=3$, $b=2$, $c=1$, $d=2$. So **$\mathbf T=\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$**.

(b) A point on $y=-x$ is $(t,-t)$ and $\mathbf T\begin{pmatrix}t\\-t\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3t-2t\\t-2t\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}t\\-t\end{pmatrix}$, which is on $y=-x$. A point on $y=\tfrac12x$ is $(2t,t)$ and $\mathbf T\begin{pmatrix}2t\\t\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}6t+2t\\2t+2t\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}8t\\4t\end{pmatrix}$, which satisfies $Y=\tfrac12X$. So **both lines are mapped onto themselves**.

(c) $\det\mathbf T=3\cdot2-2\cdot1=4$. The triangle has area $\tfrac12\cdot2\cdot3=3$, so the image has area $4\times3=$ **$12$**. (Check: the image vertices are $(0,0)$, $(6,2)$ and $(6,6)$, with area $\tfrac12|6\cdot6-2\cdot6|=12$.)

items_markdown: The image of a point is $\mathbf M\mathbf p$; the columns of $\mathbf M$ are the images of $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ (or of the three unit vectors in three dimensions), and the origin never moves.
To find the image of a line, either express $x,y$ in terms of $X,Y$ with the inverse and substitute, or map two points of the line and write the line through the images.
When $\mathbf A$ is applied first and $\mathbf B$ second, the single matrix is $\mathbf B\mathbf A$; the order matters.
$\det\mathbf M=ad-bc$: the area scale factor is $|\det\mathbf M|$, a negative sign shows reversed orientation, and a zero determinant means no inverse.
Determinants multiply for a combined transformation, and an invertible matrix sends lines to lines and lines through the origin to lines through the origin.
